source: Levi (1949) An Introduction to Legal Reasoning
finding: Founding account of reasoning by example. Three steps: find a similarity between the cases, announce the rule the first case seems to stand for, apply that rule to the new case. The rule is not fixed in advance. Each new case reshapes it, and the court decides which similarities count.
limits: Not opened this session. Described from memory and from secondary sources (Shapiro 1997; Chorley and Bench-Capon 2003). Later writers say Levi gives no test for which similarity counts.
agent_relevance: Similarity is a judgment made while reasoning, not a fixed measure. The agent needs an explicit step that names the rule behind a chosen precedent, then re-checks it on the new case.

source: Sunstein (1993) On Analogical Reasoning, 106 Harvard Law Review 741
finding: Argues analogy is the core mode of legal reasoning and needs no full theory. Features usually listed: principled consistency, focus on particulars, incompletely theorized agreements, low-level principles, tentativeness. Cases A and B are alike if a low-level principle covers both.
limits: Full text not opened (JSTOR page failed to load; only an unofficial Scribd copy exists). Features listed from memory and checked only against the Shapiro 1997 and Caputo 2026 summaries.
agent_relevance: Supports reasoning from the nearest precedent plus a modest rule, not from grand theory. Also says the rule found must stay revisable.

source: Shapiro (1997) Fear of Theory (review of Sunstein, Legal Reasoning and Political Conflict), 64 U Chicago L Rev 389
finding: Reads Sunstein's book as a Rawlsian 'method of avoidance' applied to law. Judges settle cases with rules and low-level principles that people with different deep theories can all accept (incompletely theorized agreements). The book joins three earlier law review pieces, including On Analogical Reasoning (1993).
numbers: Book is 220 pages (Oxford UP 1996). Sunstein's section on analogy is pp 62-70.
quote: People can agree that sexual discrimination is like racial discrimination and should be treated similarly without a full-fledged theory
limits: Reviewer doubts that pluralism is the real cause of incomplete theorizing. This is a reviewer's reading, not a test.
agent_relevance: A similarity call can be accepted by parties who disagree about why. The agent can accept a precedent match without proving a theory, but should record the low-level principle behind the match.

source: Caputo (2026) Alignment as Jurisprudence
finding: Compares Sunstein's analogical reasoning with case-based reasoning in AI alignment. Notes the team behind case repositories for alignment cites Sunstein, and that analogical reasoning has been shown to emerge in LLMs. Argues rules and cases depend on each other: rules take content from cases, and cases need rules to say which facts matter.
limits: Legal essay, no experiments. Cites Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) for LLM analogy, which later work challenges (see Lewis and Mitchell 2024).
agent_relevance: Legal theory gives a two-way link: cases to rule, and rule to which case facts matter. Both directions need code-checked steps.

source: Prakken and van Woerkom (2025) Defending the Hierarchical Result Models of Precedential Constraint
finding: Gives the exact formal rule for when a precedent forces a decision. Flat result model: a case base forces outcome s on fact situation F if some precedent (G,s) exists where F has at least all of G's pro-s factors and at most G's con-s factors. The hierarchical model applies the same test recursively over intermediate factors.
numbers: Definition 2.1 (flat) and 2.3 (hierarchical). A factor hierarchy has exactly one maximal element (the decision).
quote: F contains at least all Pro(s) factors that are in G and at most all Con(s) factors that are in G
limits: Pure formal work with a toy ice-cream example. No empirical test. Bench-Capon says intermediate factors can be established with different strengths, which the plain model misses.
agent_relevance: Gives a checkable, code-level meaning of 'at least as strong a case as the precedent'. This can be a program test instead of a model judgment.

source: Prakken and van Woerkom (2025) the ice-cream dispute over what makes a case 'like' another
finding: Shows the live dispute about likeness. In the MaxMonday example the same past ruling can be read as 'folded clothes beat inattentive in class' (flat) or 'behaved at home beat misbehaved at school' (hierarchical). The reading changes which new cases are bound. The authors say it depends on whether the ruling recorded the intermediate factors.
numbers: Two readings named MMF (flat) and MMH (hierarchical). A dimension-based version is proposed to answer Bench-Capon's criticism.
limits: The ratio is often not stated; later judges supply it when they cite the case.
agent_relevance: The same precedent can license different transfers. The agent must state at which level of abstraction it matches (surface facts or higher concept) before it transfers.

source: Bench-Capon and Atkinson (2021) Precedential Constraint: The Role of Issues (ICAIL 21)
finding: Reviews factor, dimension and result/reason models of precedential constraint (Horty, Rigoni, Prakken). Argues whole-case matching is wrong: cases should be split into issues. Two-stage view: first facts are mapped to factors, then factor reasoning decides. Names three precedent types: framework (structure cases into issues), preference (resolve conflicts between factor sets inside an issue), ascription (constrain the facts-to-factors mapping).
numbers: 10 pages. HYPO and CATO covered US trade secrets. IBP (Issue Based Prediction) added outcome prediction.
limits: Position paper with an illustration, not an experiment. A footnote says formal constraint may not be respected in real courts.
agent_relevance: Match precedent issue by issue, not case by case. Keep the facts-to-factors mapping as its own checked step.

source: Blass and Forbus (2023) Analogical Reasoning, Generalization, and Rule Learning for Common Law Reasoning (ICAIL 23)
finding: Applies the Structure Mapping Engine and MAC/FAC retrieval to legal cases. Builds schemas from cases with CASI (conclusion-verified analogical schema induction), then reasons three ways: direct analogy (PAPR), analogy to positive schemas (ARPG), Horn rules from schemas (RRLG). Analogy picks out legally relevant facts without hand-coded legal knowledge.
numbers: Illinois Intentional Tort dataset: 17 assault (12 pos, 5 neg), 40 battery (30 pos, 10 neg), 43 trespass (29 pos, 14 neg) = 100 cases. Probability cutoff 0.6 for schema facts.
limits: Small data, one state, cases already in predicate logic. Precision@6 uses the true answer to retry, so it is not a real-use score.
agent_relevance: Gives a computable similarity score (structure mapping) that also yields candidate inferences. Retrying with the next-best precedent after a failed check fits our retry on real output.

source: Blass and Forbus (2023) results table
finding: Rule learning from schemas was the best single-shot method. Pure analogy improved a lot with more tries and a lenient scoring test.
numbers: Overall accuracy on 100 cases: RRLG 47% (Precision@1). PAPR strict truth 17% at P@1 and 46% at P@6. PAPR partial truth 28% at P@1 and 72% at P@6 (positives 75%, negatives 66% at P@6). ARPG strict, 0 extra inferences: 28% at P@1, 35% at P@6.
limits: Of 17 cases PAPR solved at P@1 (strict), 11 were solved by analogy to an ungeneralized outlier. ARPG beat PAPR mostly on negative cases. Numbers read from a text-extracted table; treat as approximate.
agent_relevance: Outlier precedents matter: generalizing everything into one rule throws away cases that solve new ones. Keep raw precedents beside any learned rule.

source: Blass and Forbus (2023) baselines
finding: Compared with off-the-shelf language models (two BERT, two GPT models, 5-fold cross-validation) on simplified English case text. RRLG beat all baselines at P@1. All ARPG conditions beat GPT-J at P@1. Under strict truth, PAPR did not differ from GPT-J and was beaten by legalBERT. legalBERT and GPT-J beat roBERTa and GPT-2 (p < 0.0001).
numbers: Significance threshold p < 0.05. 32 conditions in all (17 variants of own methods, 5 baselines, two precision modes).
limits: Small GPT-J and BERT baselines, not 2025 frontier models.
agent_relevance: Old baseline. Do not read it as an upper limit for LLMs.

source: Blass and Forbus (2023) MAC/FAC and CASI design
finding: Retrieval is two-stage: a cheap content-vector dot product, then the structure-mapping engine on up to three candidates. SME returns alignment, candidate inferences and a similarity score. Candidate inferences that need new unbound entities (skolems) are rejected.
numbers: Up to three cases pass from MAC to FAC; up to three mappings returned.
limits: Models human memory retrieval. Needs cases in structured predicate logic.
agent_relevance: A cheap broad filter then an expensive structural match is a ready pattern for precedent retrieval, with code rejecting ungrounded inferences.

source: Chorley and Bench-Capon (2003) Developing Legal Knowledge Based Systems Through Theory Construction (ICAIL 03)
finding: Implements Bench-Capon and Sartor's view of reasoning with cases as theory construction, evaluation and application. Cases plus factors plus values give a theory; the program emits Prolog with the rule priorities the theory needs. The case study uses Aleven's CATO analysis of US trade secrets.
numbers: CATO uses 26 base-level factors. The tool generates code that enforces explicit preferences and extra preferences implied by value preferences.
limits: Case study only. The authors raise open issues, for example CATO links several factors to one value while their method links one, and the cumulative strength of factors.
agent_relevance: Treats a precedent set as a theory to build and test, not a lookup. Fits an agent that proposes a rule from cases, tests it on held-out cases, then revises.

source: Horty (2011) Rules and reasons in the theory of precedent, Legal Theory 17
finding: Formal theory of precedent. Result model: a precedent binds if the new case is at least as strong for the same side. Reason model: the court's stated reason (a rule with a priority) binds. The reason model is stricter about what a precedent says.
limits: Not opened: the PDF link failed (redirect and certificate error). Described from memory and from the 2025 Prakken paper's summary of result and reason models.
agent_relevance: Choose whether the agent treats a precedent as an outcome to match or as a stated reason to apply. Reason-based is easier to audit.

source: Rissland and Ashley (1987) HYPO; Ashley (1990); Aleven (2003) CATO
finding: HYPO builds a three-step argument: cite the most on-point precedent (most shared factors), distinguish it, rebut. CATO adds a factor hierarchy so similarities and distinctions can be argued at a higher level, for example downplaying or emphasizing a distinction.
numbers: Abstract of Aleven (2003): arguments about the significance of distinctions helped predict outcomes in trade secrets cases; a legal writing course study favoured CATO instruction over best traditional instruction.
limits: Not opened. Taken from a search-result abstract and from the Blass and Zhang papers. Aleven and Ashley (1997) is reported to have found CATO students less prepared for a memo assignment.
agent_relevance: A ready scheme for the operator: retrieve closest precedent, list unshared factors, argue whether each distinction matters, then answer.

source: Zhang, Grabmair, Gray and Ashley (2026) Thinking Longer, Not Always Smarter: LLMs in Hierarchical Legal Reasoning (CSLAW 26)
finding: Tests reasoning models on a CATO-based three-task chain about distinctions between a current case and a precedent. Surface identification is solved. Hierarchical reasoning is weaker. Integrated analysis of all significant distinctions collapses.
numbers: 253 test instances per task, each with 4 current-case factors and 4 precedent factors. Task 1: 100% for all 6 models. Task 2: 64.82% (gemini-2.5-flash) to 92.09% (gpt-5). Task 3: 11.46% to 33.99%, most under 25%. 5 reasoning models plus 1 non-reasoning.
limits: Synthetic factor sets from the CATO trade-secrets hierarchy, not real briefs. The PDF table extracts misaligned, so per-model pairing may be off; ranges come from the text.
agent_relevance: Listing differences is easy for models; deciding which differences matter, using the hierarchy, is the weak step. Put the significance step under code-checked rules.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) distinction task definitions
finding: Gives code-checkable definitions for the HYPO/CATO moves. A distinction is an unshared factor that makes the precedent a weaker analogy. Task 2 asks for the argumentative support of a distinction through the hierarchy; Task 3 asks which distinctions are significant. Scoring is exact set match.
numbers: Exact-set-match accuracy; Definition 5 (distinction) and Definition 10 (emphasizing a distinction).
quote: A distinction is an unshared factor that indicates the precedent case (C2) is not a perfect analogy for the current case (C1)
limits: Strict exact-set scoring may understate partial credit.
agent_relevance: The distinction step can be computed by code (set difference of factors). Only the significance judgment needs the model.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) thinking versus non-thinking and token cost
finding: Thinking helps, but longer thinking is not better thinking. Models spend more tokens on wrong answers than on right ones.
numbers: qwen3-235b thinking 78.66% on Task 2 vs 30.04% non-thinking (2.6x); on Task 3 33.99% vs 0.00%. gpt-5 used about 4,456 tokens on wrong Task 2 answers vs 3,081 on right (45% more). Task 3 thinking tokens reach about 15,000 for some models.
limits: Token counts are per-instance averages. Only one non-reasoning comparison model.
agent_relevance: Supports G1: do not add doubt or more thinking on a schedule. Use failed checks, not length, as the signal.

source: Zou, Zhang, Weir, Van Durme and Holzenberger (2024) Reasoning by analogy for tax-law entailment (arXiv 2401.06715)
finding: Recasts statutory reasoning as analogy: two (statute, case) pairs are analogous if both have the same entailment label. Models stayed near chance. Retrieving similar cases and majority-voting analogy predictions gave a small gain that was not significant.
numbers: SARA tax-law data. GPT zero-shot 49 to 59% (gpt-4-0613 68 +/- 3 with one prompt variant). 6-shot 49 to 56%. Hand-made CoT 53 to 59%. Vector offset about 50%. T5-Large 53.3% dev, 50.7% test. Retrieval plus analogy best 57% (DPR). Majority baseline 50%.
limits: One domain, small test set, gain not significant, only 5 cases in the behaviour analysis. The page gives inconsistent dataset sizes, so size numbers are uncertain.
agent_relevance: A bare LLM call on whether two cases are analogous is close to a coin flip here. Do not trust it without a check.

source: Fan et al. (2025/2026) Legal Rule Induction from Analogous Judicial Precedents (arXiv 2505.14104)
finding: Defines the task of inducing a rule (precondition, behaviour, consequence) from a set of analogous cases. Frontier models over-generalize and hallucinate. Fine-tuning small models on the new data gives big gains.
numbers: 5,121 case sets (38,088 court cases) for tuning, 216 expert gold sets, Chinese law. Llama-3.2-3B micro-F1 19.21% to 70.96% after LoRA. Ministral-8B + LoRA micro-F1 73.18%, macro-F1 70.73%, above Gemini-2.5-Flash direct 60.51% and Claude-3.7-Sonnet direct 66.67%. Abstract states over 76% F1 gains.
limits: Chinese criminal law; rules are model-written then matched by elements, so the metric depends on that matching. Civil-law setting, not common-law stare decisis.
agent_relevance: Inducing the rule that links analogous cases is hard for LLMs. A checkable rule format (condition, behaviour, consequence) makes it testable.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Mitigating Legal Hallucinations via Symbolic Constraints and Analogical Precedents (AALawyer, ACL 2026)
finding: Dual retrieval. One part retrieves statutes under a symbolic constraint. The other, Analogical Precedent Retrieval, finds similar criminal cases to support the facts. The authors say plain dense retrieval fails by semantic drift: vivid surface wording (crowbar, beating) pulls in the wrong article.
numbers: Against base DeepSeek-7B: hallucination risk down 37.6%, professionalism +13.4%, informativeness +41.9%, explainability +43.4%, mean score +34.1%. Symbolic retrieval precision 89.67%, recall 84.26% on 200 samples. Criminal-article classification +71.98% over the base.
limits: Chinese criminal law; partly LLM-judged (Table 7 meta-evaluation); self-built HR-Benchmark. Percent gains are relative to a weak 7B base.
agent_relevance: Names the failure we care about: likeness by word overlap picks the wrong precedent. Retrieval must match the abstract legal feature, not the vivid facts.

source: Chen and Zhang (2025) Case Law Grounding: Using Precedents to Align Decision-Making for Humans and AI (CI 2025)
finding: Replaces written rules (constitutions) with retrieved past decisions as grounding for subjective decisions (content moderation, toxicity). Three steps: retrieve cases, select applicable precedents, decide. Works for human groups and LLMs.
numbers: Reddit comment moderation and toxicity rating; 3 Reddit communities (n=35) and 2 demographic groups (n=60). Humans: gains of +16.0 to +23.3 percentage points in 4 of 5 groups (p 0.010 to 0.045). LLM: +20.8 to +32.9 pp in 4 of 5 groups (p 0.004 to 0.011). AmItheAsshole group: +10.6 pp, not significant (p=0.229).
limits: Subjective labelling tasks, not law. The authors report that binding decisions and larger retrieval windows helped; exact window values not recorded here.
agent_relevance: Retrieved precedents with binding force beat rule lists in these tasks. Fits an agent that carries a case memory and checks new answers against it.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour 7
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat UCLA undergraduates on text matrix reasoning, letter-string and verbal analogies, zero-shot. It was worse than students on story analogies that need causal (higher-order) relations across different domains.
numbers: Digit matrices (humans N=40): GPT-3 better, OR=1.88, p=0.005 (generative); OR=6.27 (multiple choice). Letter strings (N=57): OR=1.76, p=6.3e-5. Story analogies (N=54): students clearly better, OR=0.37, p=0.0003; GPT-3 not above chance on far analogy (p=0.065); 15 of 54 students picked the causal match on every trial.
limits: Tests may be in training data (Hodel and West). Story analogy is closest to legal likeness, and it is where GPT-3 was weakest. GPT-4 was reported better only in a preliminary check.
agent_relevance: Surface similarity is easy for LLMs. Matching by shared causal structure across different facts is the harder, legally relevant case.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using Counterfactual Tasks to Evaluate the Generality of Analogical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Failed generalization of Webb et al. Same letter-string analogies, but with permuted or symbol alphabets. Humans stay high; GPT-3, 3.5 and 4 drop sharply. Many GPT errors come from using an alternate rule.
numbers: Human sample 46 here vs 57 in Webb. Alternate-rule errors: 38.59% of GPT-3.5 errors, 22% of GPT-4, 5.81% of GPT-3. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 were no better than GPT-3 on these problems.
limits: Letter-string domain only. Overall accuracy figures were not read from the figures, only error shares from the text.
agent_relevance: LLM analogy leans on familiar patterns. A precedent with unfamiliar wording may fail even when its structure matches. Test the match on a mutated version (G3).

source: Hodel and West (2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Argues Webb et al.'s zero-shot claim cannot be shown, since the problems may be in training data, and that tests made for humans may not measure LLM ability. Shows GPT-3 fails simple variants of the original tasks while humans stay high.
quote: GPT-3 fails to solve simplest variations of the original tasks, whereas human performance remains consistently high
limits: Short response with a small appendix experiment. The authors note Webb et al. disclosed the contamination risk in peer review.
agent_relevance: Do not claim an LLM can do analogy from one benchmark win. Use new, held-out cases.

source: Caputo (2026) rules and cases (Hart's no-vehicles example)
finding: Uses Hart's two devices (rules and precedent) and the no-vehicles-in-the-park example: a rule's content comes from examples applied by analogy to new, unforeseen cases. More elaborate rule text cannot fix this in novel cases.
limits: Essay. No measurements.
agent_relevance: Explains why a rule list alone fails on edge cases and why a case memory is a needed second source.
